name: Question 14
worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -7 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that E1 and E2 are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find E2−1. We write down E2 and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[E2|I]=[10101101]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[101001−11]

Therefore,

E2−1=[10−11].

Now, we can find the product E1E2−1:

E1E2−1=[10−61][10−11]=[10−71]
